analysis.one_liner: Makes the 2017 tax law's individual rate cuts, bigger standard deduction, and other tax breaks permanent.
analysis.headline: A bill to make the 2017 tax law's individual tax cuts permanent died in the Ways and Means Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2017 Republican tax law cut individual income tax rates (including a new top rate of 37%), enlarged the standard deduction, limited itemized deductions, and raised the alternative minimum tax exemption — but those individual provisions were scheduled to expire after 2025. This bill would have written them into the tax code permanently, and in several places gone further, such as repealing the limit on itemized deductions entirely and applying the new brackets to capital gains. It never received a hearing or a vote; it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and died there when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: High-income households gain the most: permanent 37% top rates, permanent repeal of the itemized-deduction limit, and a much larger alternative minimum tax exemption apply mostly to filers at the top of the income scale [S3]. Middle-income families also keep the lower rates and the larger standard deduction, which simplifies filing for people who don't itemize [S2]. Investors and owners of pass-through businesses gain from the lower rates applied to capital gains and business income [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It permanently keeps the lower income tax rates created by the 2017 tax law, including a top rate of 37% instead of 39.6%.
It permanently raises the standard deduction to $18,000 for individuals and $12,000 for others, which simplifies filing and benefits taxpayers who don't itemize.

It permanently repeals the limit on itemized deductions and raises the alternative minimum tax exemption to $109,400 for joint filers, which mainly reduces taxes for high-income households that itemize heavily or face the AMT.

analysis.who_pays: If the cuts are not offset, everyone bears them through larger federal deficits and the future tax increases or program cuts that follow; since the bill offers no pay-fors, the cost is deferred rather than eliminated [S3].

drawbacks.text: Making the TCJA's individual rate cuts permanent would reduce federal revenue by hundreds of billions of dollars per decade, and the bill contains no offsetting tax increases or spending cuts, so the cost lands on the deficit or on future taxpayers.

Repealing the limit on itemized deductions and locking in the 37% top rate directs the largest dollar benefits to high earners, since itemized deductions are concentrated among wealthier taxpayers and the top bracket applies only to income above roughly $600,000 for couples.

The bill quietly applies the income-tax-bracket changes to capital gains as well, lowering the threshold at which the higher 20% capital gains rate applies in some cases — a technical change that mostly affects large investment gains.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For upper-income households and pass-through business owners, making the cuts permanent is a clear financial win. For everyone else, the honest accounting is that the same individual rates, standard deduction, and AMT relief are already scheduled to expire, so the bill's practical effect is mostly to extend tax cuts weighted toward the top — and to do so with no identified way to pay for the lost revenue, which shifts the burden toward future spending cuts, future tax increases elsewhere, or deficits [S2][S3]. It is a one-sided bill whose largest gains go to the people who already pay the highest tax rates.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and sat there until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Schweikert introduced the bill on June 23, 2022, with 14 Republican cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee the same day, the only action ever taken on it.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, with the bill never reported out of committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy taxpayers were spared no loss, since the 2017 tax cuts were already in effect; the bill's death simply preserved the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the existing tax code simply stayed as it was

for.name: Rep. David Schweikert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the 2017 tax law's individual provisions permanent.

for.name: 14 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 14 cosponsors were Republicans.

sides.party_line_note: All sponsorship and all 14 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported it [S4].

industries.note: Locking in the 37% top rate, repealing the itemized-deduction limit, and raising the AMT exemption all deliver the largest dollar savings at the top of the income scale [S3].
The bill applies the new brackets to capital gains and repeals rate limits for corporations, and high earners who own businesses benefit most from the permanent lower rates [S3].
Middle-income filers also keep the lower rates and larger standard deduction, though the 2017 law tilted its benefits toward the top and the bill pays for none of it [S2].
